title: Deutsche Prostatakarzinom-Früherkennungs-Kohorten-Studie zur Evaluation einer risikobasierten Bildgebung-Biopsie Strategie
summary:
Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common cancer in men, with 79,600 new cases and 15,200 deaths annually.
For early detection, the PSA (prostate-specific antigen) blood test is one of the methods used. PSA-based screening can prevent deaths from prostate cancer. However, it can also lead to overdiagnosis, in which tumors are detected that would not have caused any symptoms without the test. This can result in unnecessary MRI scans, tissue samples (biopsies), and treatments with potential side effects.
The current German S3 guideline therefore recommends a stepwise approach. If PSA levels are repeatedly elevated (≥ 3 ng/ml), the individual’s risk is first assessed based on various factors. Depending on the risk, an MRI scan of the prostate may then be performed. If the MRI reveals suspicious changes, a targeted biopsy may be performed. During the first biopsy, tissue samples are also collected systematically. This approach is intended to avoid unnecessary biopsies and the treatment of clinically insignificant tumors.
For individual risk assessment, the guideline recommends, among other tools, two scientifically validated risk calculators: the Rotterdam Prostate Cancer Risk Calculator (RPCRC) and the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial Risk Calculator (PCPTRC) 2.0. These calculators use various patient-specific data to estimate the probability of prostate cancer. However, they were developed before MRI became a routine part of the diagnostic process. Therefore, it is not yet sufficiently clear at what calculated risk level an MRI scan—and, if necessary, a biopsy—should be performed.
The aim of this study is to investigate whether risk-adapted diagnosis using these risk calculators detects prostate cancer of higher clinical significance just as reliably as an approach involving routine MRI. At the same time, the study aims to determine whether this approach can help avoid unnecessary MRI scans and prostate biopsies.
In this study, clinically significant prostate cancer is defined as a tumor of ISUP Grade Group 2 (GG2) or higher. In addition, the risk calculators used will be compared in terms of their diagnostic accuracy and their ability to classify patients according to their individual risk.
The two diagnostic approaches are compared in the same participants. This allows for a reduction in differences between individuals and enables a direct assessment of diagnostic accuracy as well as the potential to avoid unnecessary tests.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
•	Men between the ages of ≥50 and <70 who wish to undergo prostate cancer screening (after being informed about the benefits and risks of the test and its consequences)
•	Clinical suspicion of PCa based on a confirmed PSA level of ≥ 3 ng/ml (at least 2 consecutive readings of ≥ 3 ng/ml within 3 months)
•	Life expectancy of at least 10 years
•	Willingness to undergo a DRE and a transrectal ultrasound (TRUS)
•	Willingness to undergo a prostate biopsy in accordance with local standards (transrectal or transperineal) if MRI imaging reveals abnormal findings
•	Written informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
•	Known PCa or a PSA level ≥ 30 ng/ml within the last 3 months
•	Previous prostate biopsy within the last 4 years
•	Previous prostate MRI showing a PI-RADS 3–5 lesion within the last 4 years
•	Previous prostate surgery for benign prostatic syndrome within the last 5 years (including interventional procedures such as UroLift™, Rezüm™, stents, etc.)
•	Contraindications for undergoing an MRI (e.g., due to metal implants)
•	Contraindications to performing a DRE or a TRUS (to determine prostate volume)
•	Contraindications to performing a transrectal or transperineal prostate biopsy
•	Known pathogenic germline mutation in one of the following genes: BRCA2, MSH2, MSH6
